source.name: Post-punk
source.lineage: Late-1970s through early-1980s underground rock movement extending punk's rejection of rock-tradition conventions through more harmonic-and-rhythmic experimentation, dub-and-disco bass-and-rhythm sensibility, and intellectualized lyrical content — codified through Wire (Pink Flag 1977), Joy Division (Unknown Pleasures 1979), Gang of Four (Entertainment! 1979), The Fall, Public Image Ltd (Metal Box 1979), Magazine, Talking Heads (Remain in Light 1980)

Defined by angular-bass-led grooves where bass-foundation often becomes the song's melodic-foreground rather than a rhythm-section foundation, dissonant chord voicings and modal-and-atonal harmonic vocabulary departing from punk's three-chord-vocabulary, treble-heavy guitar tone with chorus-and-flanger effects, processed and treated drum-sounds (often emphasizing snare and floor-tom over kit-foundation), lyrical content addressing political-and-philosophical subjects rather than punk's nihilist-confrontational stance, and song-form often extended beyond punk's 2-3-minute economy with experimental structural ambition. Distinguished from punk by art-music ambition and rejection of three-chord-vocabulary; distinguished from new wave by darker mood and absence of pop-craft commercial orientation; distinguished from gothic rock by absence of romantic-melodrama-and-occult lyrical apparatus.

source.name: Doom metal
source.lineage: Doom metal as broad genre family descended from the Black Sabbath template — covering traditional doom (Pentagram, Saint Vitus, Candlemass), funeral doom (the slowest variant, 30-40 BPM, Mournful Congregation, Esoteric, Skepticism), the Electric Wizard / Cathedral UK occult-doom canon, and stoner-doom (psychedelic-sub-elements through Sleep, Electric Wizard, Bongripper) — distinct from the New Orleans sludge-and-hardcore axis covered by sludge metal and distinct from the sustained-tone minimalism covered by drone metal

extras.description: Doom metal (1970 onward, with first-wave English heavy-blues-rock origin through Black Sabbath's eponymous 1970 debut and a 1980s second-wave codification through Saint Vitus, Pentagram, and Trouble), the slow-tempo downtuned-and-sustained heavy metal subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed down to 60-80 BPM with sustained chord-and-riff durations stretching past five minutes, downtuned guitars (D-standard, drop-C, drop-B) producing thicker low-end heaviness, vocal delivery alternating clean-melodic with growled (subgenre-dependent), heavy reverb-and-fuzz guitar tone preserving extended sustain, lyric and visual themes of occult, mortality, and existential dread, and song-form built on slow riff-progression rather than verse-chorus pop structure. Subgenres include traditional doom (clean vocals, heavy-blues), funeral doom (extreme slowness past 40 BPM), and stoner doom (psychedelic sub-elements). Distinguished from heavy metal by tempo; distinguished from drone metal by retention of song-form structure rather than sustained-tone minimalism; distinguished from sludge metal by absence of hardcore-punk-derived aggression and New Orleans regional lineage; distinguished from black-metal atmospheric by absence of blast-beat foundation.

extras.description: Emo (codified mid-1980s onward through DC-and-Midwest-and-late-1990s American post-hardcore scenes; first wave 1985-1990 in DC-hardcore scene through Rites of Spring 1985 establishing the emotionally-confessional lyric foregrounding within hardcore-punk foundation, with Embrace 1985 and Beefeater extending the lineage; second wave 1993-2001 Midwest-emo through Sunny Day Real Estate Diary 1994, Cap'n Jazz Analphabetapolothology, Mineral Power of Failing 1997, American Football American Football 1999, The Promise Ring 30° Everywhere 1996, Texas Is the Reason Do You Know Who You Are? 1996 establishing the Midwest-emo intricate-clean-guitar-arpeggio + dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song-architecture vocabulary; third wave 2000-2008 mainstream-crossover through Jimmy Eat World Bleed American 2001, Dashboard Confessional The Places You Have Come to Fear the Most 2001, My Chemical Romance Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge 2004, Fall Out Boy From Under the Cork Tree 2005 bringing emo to mainstream-radio prominence; fourth wave 2008-onward revival including The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die, Modern Baseball, and 2020s-onward contemporary emo continuation), the mid-1980s through present-day post-hardcore-derived rock subgenre defined by emotionally-confessional lyric content and dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song architecture. Defined by emotionally-confessional lyric content (first-person confessional lyric register addressing depression, anxiety, romantic-heartbreak, social-alienation themes — the genre-defining lyric-content orientation that distinguishes emo from pop-punk's adolescent-romance content and from hardcore-punk's political-content), dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song architecture (the Midwest-emo song-form alternating intricate clean-guitar-arpeggio quiet sections with full-band distorted-power-chord loud sections, distinguishing emo from straight-pop-punk's sustained-distortion approach), intricate clean-guitar-arpeggio textural work (the Midwest-emo math-rock-influenced finger-tapped-and-arpeggiated clean-electric-guitar vocabulary), vocal-delivery alternating between sung-melodic-introspection and shouted-cathartic-emotional-release (often called the emo-scream technique), and song-forms ranging from short pop-emo verse-chorus to extended Midwest-emo through-composed architecture. Distinguished from preceding hardcore-punk by emotional-confessional lyric foregrounding vs political-content foregrounding; distinguished from contemporaneous pop-punk by introspective-confessional lyric register vs pop-punk's extroverted-adolescent register and clean-guitar-arpeggio textural foreground vs pop-punk's sustained-distortion approach; distinguished from later screamo by song-melodic-foregrounding vs screamo's scream-and-noise-dominated approach.

source.name: Goth
source.lineage: Formed 1979-1985 out of British post-punk around the Batcave club in London and Leeds' Merrion Centre scene — Bauhaus, Siouxsie and the Banshees, The Sisters of Mercy and The Cure established flanged and chorused single-coil guitar drenched in long plate and digital reverb, high-mixed chorused bass carrying the riff, tribal floor-tom or drum-machine patterns at 100-140 BPM, and baritone or keening declamatory vocals over minor and Phrygian modal harmony.

extras.description: Goth crystallized in Britain between 1979 and 1985 as post-punk's darkest, most theatrical branch, built on reverb-saturated chorused guitar, prominent melodic bass, and either tom-led tribal drumming or a rigidly programmed drum machine. Harmony stays in minor and Phrygian territory with sustained pedal tones, and vocals are delivered in a low theatrical baritone or a high wailing register with heavy vibrato. It is distinguished from generic post-punk by its committed aesthetic of decay and ritual, and from later industrial and darkwave by remaining guitar-centered rather than synthesizer-driven.

source.name: Digital Hardcore
source.lineage: Coined in Berlin in 1993 by Alec Empire, who founded the Digital Hardcore Recordings label and Atari Teenage Riot to fuse hardcore punk's shouted political sloganeering with 180-220 BPM breakbeat programming — Amen and Funky Drummer breaks pushed into clipping distortion, downtuned electric guitar riffs cut into sampler-triggered stabs, screamed dual male-female vocals in German and English, and an anti-fascist agitprop lyric stance shaped by the post-reunification squat scene.

extras.description: Digital hardcore was invented in Berlin in 1993 as an explicit collision of punk ideology and rave technology, most visibly through Alec Empire's Digital Hardcore Recordings roster and Atari Teenage Riot. The sound is defined by breakbeats sampled to the point of clipping and red-lined through cheap gear, downtuned guitar stabs treated as percussion, tempos between 180 and 220 BPM, and shouted or screamed political vocals traded between two singers rather than sung hooks. It is distinguished from gabber by its punk band roster and guitar content, from breakcore by its song-shaped verse-chorus scaffolding, and from industrial rock by using samplers rather than a live rhythm section.
